### Mohieddin Jafari {.mt-3}

**University of Helsinki and Tampere University**

*A systems pharmacology approach for combinatorial therapy*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}

## Abstract

Drug combinations hold promise but are often selected empirically, with limited
mechanistic understanding. We developed Combinatorial Proteome Integral
Solubility/Stability Alteration analysis (CoPISA), a high-throughput proteomics
platform that captures protein-level effects uniquely induced by drug
combinations. Applying CoPISA to rationally designed drug pairs, we uncovered
an emergent mechanism we term “conjunctional targeting,” in which combinations
engage exclusive protein targets consistent with an AND-gate logic. By
revealing a mechanistic layer beyond classical synergy, CoPISA provides a
systems pharmacology framework for the rational design of combinatorial
therapies across complex diseases.
:::

::::

:::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6 .g-col-lg-4 .d-flex .flex-column}

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DELQE1zIgTc >}}

### Dennis Völkl {.mt-3}

**University of Bergen**

*HIDE: Hierarchical Cell Type Deconvolution*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}

## Abstract

The video presents HIDE, a method to estimate cell-type proportions from bulk
transcriptomics while explicitly using a cell-type hierarchy. Instead of
deconvolving all cell types at once (which can be unstable when references are
highly correlated), HIDE proceeds top-down: it first estimates broad
populations, then iteratively refines into subtypes within each parent, using
“residual” bulks so child proportions remain consistent with the parent total.
The method also learns gene weights (trained using pseudo-bulks from
single-cell data) to improve deconvolution accuracy at each hierarchy level.
The key benefit is more robust and interpretable estimates—upper-level
proportions stay reliable even if fine-grained subtypes are hard to
resolve—while still enabling subtype resolution when the signal supports it.
:::

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8gX7q18jC90 >}}

### Arber Qoku {.mt-3}

**German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ)**

*MOFA-FLEX: A Factor Model Language for Integrating Omics Data with Prior Knowledge*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}

## Abstract

Latent factor models are essential tools for analyzing omics data and are often
the starting point for single- and multi-omics studies. However, adapting these
models to complex experimental designs involving spatial, temporal, or
multimodal data typically requires significant statistical expertise and
development effort. We introduce MOFA-FLEX, a modular and extensible Bayesian
factor analysis framework built on probabilistic programming. MOFA-FLEX
integrates and generalizes components from various matrix factorization
methods, allowing users to combine flexible priors (e.g., structured sparsity,
covariate-informed), non-negativity constraints, supervision signals, and
diverse data likelihoods. It also introduces a novel sparsity prior for
incorporating biological knowledge, such as gene sets or pathway signatures,
enabling interpretable latent factors linked to biological processes. We
demonstrate MOFA-FLEX across multiple use cases, including (i) robust recovery
of gene sets (gene programs) in noisy scRNA-seq data using imperfect priors,
(ii) disentangling technical and biological variation in multi-omics studies,
and (iii) modeling spatial omics data to map disease-associated gene activity
in breast cancer. Ultimately, MOFA-FLEX streamlines the creation of tailored
and interpretable models for diverse omics applications.
:::

### Alexandru Tomescu {.mt-3}

**University of Helsinki**

*Decomposing a weighted graph into few paths for solving multi-assembly problems*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Abstract

A multi-assembly problem usually asks us to decompose a weighted graph into a
small number of weighted paths.

For example, in the RNA transcript assembly problem, the graph nodes are gene
exons, the weights are read coverages, and the edges indicate connections
between exons observed in RNA-seq reads. The weighted paths are the RNA
transcripts, together with their expression levels, that need to be identified
from the RNA-seq reads.

Such problems easily become NP-hard, and many RNA assembly tools therefore
solve them heuristically.

In this talk, I give an overview of our recent results on extremely fast and
exact solvers for a range of such decomposition problems. These are based on
Mixed Integer Linear Programming and benefit from additional “safety
optimizations” based on insights into the simpler parts of the graph structure.

These results are currently being incorporated into a Python package so that
developers of future multi-assembly tools can easily use exact and accurate
decomposition methods.
:::

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J0n-Xwyr7RM >}}

### Dr. Jing Tang {.mt-3}

**University of Helsinki**

*Advanced computational and experimental methods to tackle drug resistance in cancer*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Abstract

Despite scientific advances, options for treating cancer patients are still
limited, especially after relapse. To achieve more sustainable treatment
efficacy, patients will need novel drug targets and combination therapies.
However, the lack of understanding on cancer-drug interactions prevents
biomarker discovery and ultimately leads to high attrition in clinical trials.
In this talk, I will introduce multiple systems medicine approaches for the
prediction of drug targets, the prediction of drug sensitivity, and the
prediction of drug combinations. I will explore: 1) whether the
loss-of-function genetic screen technologies such as CRISPR or RNAi can help
identify cancer dependency map; 2) whether the integration of loss-of-function
genetic and drug sensitivity screening data could help identify the mechanisms
of action of drugs; and 3) whether the drug target interaction and drug
sensitivity data can help predict synergistic drug combinations. Finally, I
will show the potential of lineage tracing data to inform an evidence-based
treatment decision.
:::

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gRVHLu7MoI0 >}}

### Chengbo Fu {.mt-3}

**Aalto University**

*KMAP: Kmer Manifold Approximation and Projection for visualizing DNA sequences*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Abstract

Identifying and illustrating patterns in DNA sequences is a crucial task in
various biological data analyses. In this task, patterns are often represented
by sets of kmers, the fundamental building blocks of DNA sequences.

To visually unveil these patterns, we could project each kmer onto a point in
two-dimensional space. However, this projection poses challenges because of the
high-dimensional nature of kmers and their unique mathematical properties.

We established a mathematical system to address the peculiarities of the kmer
manifold. Leveraging this theory, we developed a statistical method named KMAP
for detecting kmer patterns and visualizing them in two-dimensional space.

We applied KMAP to three distinct datasets to showcase its utility. KMAP
achieved performance comparable to the classical method MEME, with
approximately 90% similarity in motif discovery from HT-SELEX data.

In the analysis of H3K27ac ChIP-seq data from Ewing Sarcoma, we found that
BACH1, OTX2, and ERG1 might affect prognosis by binding to promoter and
enhancer regions across the genome. We also found that FLI1 bound to enhancer
regions after ETV6 degradation, indicating competitive binding between ETV6 and
FLI1.

Moreover, KMAP identified four prevalent patterns in gene-editing data from the
AAVS1 locus, aligning with findings reported in the literature.

These applications underscore that KMAP could be a valuable tool across various
biological contexts.
:::

### Thaddeus Wu {.mt-3}

**James Cook University, Australia**

*Behind the Transcriptomic Complexity*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Abstract

Recent advances in single-cell long-read sequencing have revolutionised our
understanding of transcriptomic complexity.

However, traditional analysis pipelines designed for short-read sequencing fail
to capture the full complexity of isoform-level information.

In this talk, I introduce our ongoing project: a novel computational framework
that addresses these challenges. Using early blood development as a model
system, we demonstrate interesting findings and insights that help us
understand transcriptomic complexity.
:::

### Luca Musella {.mt-3}

**University Hospital Erlangen, Julio Vera Laboratory, Germany**

*ENQUIRE reconstructs and expands context-specific co-occurrence networks from biomedical literature*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Abstract

The accelerating growth of scientific literature overwhelms our capacity to
manually distil complex phenomena such as molecular networks linked to
diseases. Moreover, biases in biomedical research and database annotation limit
our interpretation of facts and generation of hypotheses.

ENQUIRE—Expanding Networks by Querying Unexpected
